title: NUMERICAL STUDY OF MAGNETOHYDRODYNAMIC BIOCONVECTIVE FLOW OVER A CURVED SURFACE WITH RADIATION AND THERMAL SOLUTAL EFFECTS
journal: Journal of Mechanics in Medicine and Biology
abstract: This study investigates the influence of chemical species on magnetized bioconvection flow of a viscous nanofluid over a stretching curved surface. The analysis incorporates the effects of Brownian motion, Thermophoresis, Thermal radiation, and internal heat generation/absorption. Convective thermal and solutal boundary conditions are imposed to examine heat and mass transport characteristics. Appropriate similarity transformations are employed to convert the governing partial differential equations into a system of nonlinear ordinary differential equations, which are then solved numerically using the BVP4C scheme. The results indicate that an increase in the magnetic field parameter significantly suppresses the velocity gradient due to the Lorentz force. Moreover, simultaneous enhancement of thermal radiation and Brownian motion parameters leads to a pronounced rise in the temperature distribution. The concentration gradient is found to increase with higher values of the solutal Biot number and Brownian motion parameter. Additionally, the local density number, Nusselt number, and Sherwood number are computed and analyzed. A comparative assessment with previously published results in limiting cases is presented, demonstrating excellent agreement and validating the accuracy of the numerical methodology. This study presents a novel unified numerical framework that simultaneously incorporates bioconvection, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal radiation, and thermo-solutal effects over a curved surface, addressing the lack of comprehensive analyses of these coupled phenomena in existing literature. The findings provide new insights into the interaction between curvature, magnetic fields, heat transfer, mass transfer, and microorganism dynamics. The proposed model has potential applications in biomedical engineering, bio-reactors, solar thermal systems, microfluidic devices, and advanced heat and mass transfer technologies.

title: When social pedagogy goes to school: innovative approaches promoting agency, community and democracy in formal education
Value co-creation pathways for construction waste reduction
abstract: Purpose This study aims to address the persistent challenges of fragmented collaboration and unclear value exchange in construction waste reduction (CWR). It seeks to develop a systematic understanding of how stakeholders collaborate by constructing a stakeholder value network (SVN) model. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-methods approach was employed, integrating value co-creation and social exchange theory. The SVN model was developed and analyzed using data from a literature review, policy analysis and semi-structured expert interviews. The network analysis identified 45 value streams and 846 value loops, with robustness ensured through sensitivity analysis. Findings The results reveal that non-economic values, specifically knowledge sharing, policy support and social recognition, play a more critical structural role than financial incentives in sustaining collaborative networks. Furthermore, contractors, owners and designers form the triadic core of CWR governance, whereas suppliers and the public assume more peripheral roles than traditionally presumed. Originality/value This study contributes a novel, network-based analytical framework for examining multi-stakeholder cooperation in sustainability-oriented projects. It challenges the conventional overemphasis on economic drivers as the primary collaborative force and redefines core governance actors. Based on the findings, a government-led guarantee mechanism is proposed to strengthen cross-sector collaboration, providing actionable strategies for policymakers and project managers to optimize value exchange and enhance CWR performance.

title: Uncorking change: female leadership and sustainable transformation in the Chilean wine industry
journal: International Journal of Wine Business Research
abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore how women leaders in the Chilean wine industry describe and enact leadership practices in relation to sustainability-oriented management. It further examines the organizational and sector-specific conditions that enable or constrain these practices in a historically male-dominated industry. Design/methodology/approach This qualitative, interpretive study used semi-structured interviews with 16 women leaders in the Chilean wine industry, analyzed through hybrid thematic analysis combining deductive and inductive coding, supported by ATLAS.ti 23. Findings Participants described relational, participatory and long-term-oriented leadership practices linked to sustainability-oriented management, including employee engagement, capacity-building, formalized environmental routines and interorganizational collaboration. Implementation depended on decision-making authority, organizational resources, senior-management support and sectoral pressures. Findings are exploratory and do not establish that these practices are exclusive to women or causally linked to sustainability. Research limitations/implications The study focuses exclusively on women leaders in the Chilean wine industry, limiting generalizability. Future research could incorporate comparative perspectives across sectors, countries and gender groups, and longitudinal analyses of sustainability-oriented leadership. Practical implications Findings highlight the value of inclusive leadership development, transparent promotion systems, mentoring networks and gender-sensitive policies to strengthen sustainable management in the wine sector. Social implications By linking gender-inclusive leadership to sustainability transitions, the study reinforces the relevance of SDG 5 – gender equality and SDG 8 – decent work and economic growth, emphasizing women’s leadership in fostering more equitable, sustainable organizations. Originality/value This study integrates female leadership, gender equality and sustainable management in an emerging-economy wine sector, extending Grimstad’s (2011) framework by examining how women leaders describe relational and long-term-oriented practices as resources that may support sustainability-oriented management under specific institutional conditions.

title: Triterpenoid saponins from the aerial parts of Phytolacca americana and their anti-influenza A virus activity
abstract: Abstract Phytolacca americana L. (Phytolaccaceae), a perennial species native to North America, is rich in oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins. In this study, ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC–QTOF–MS) profiling of the aerial-part extract revealed characteristic fragment ions of phytolaccagenin- and phytolaccagenic acid-type saponins with diverse glycosylation. MS-guided annotation enabled targeted isolation and structural elucidation of two previously undescribed compounds, one oleanane-type triterpenoid saponin (1) and one neolignan (3). Additionally, compound 2, which had been reported only based on mass spectrometric data, was isolated, and its structure was fully elucidated for the first time, together with those of 10 known oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins (4–13). Their structures were elucidated by comprehensive one-dimensional and two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopic analyses combined with UPLC–QTOF–MS data. Although P. americana extracts have been reported to inhibit influenza A virus infection in previous studies, the bioactive constituents responsible for this antiviral activity have not been identified. The crude extract and isolated saponins were evaluated using complementary in vitro assays. In H1N1-infected A549 cells, compound 11 (3-O-trisaccharide phytolaccagenic acid) reduced viral NS1 RNA levels at 6 and 24 hpi as determined by RT–qPCR. Antiviral activity was further confirmed by plaque reduction and immunoblot analyses, with a plaque-assay IC50 of 57.98 ± 0.26 µM.

title: The entrepreneurial and engaged university: development and validation of a faculty perception scale
journal: Journal of Small Business and Enterprise Development
abstract: Purpose The modern university is increasingly mandated to move beyond its traditional missions and act as a core engine for regional development. This has given rise to the concepts of the “entrepreneurial” and “socially engaged” university. However, existing metrics often focus narrowly on quantitative outputs, failing to capture the underlying institutional culture. This paper addresses this gap by developing and validating a novel instrument to measure the entrepreneurial and engaged university through faculty perceptions. Design/methodology/approach Based on a review of the literature, a perception-based scale was developed. The instrument was then validated using a sample of 186 university professors from various Brazilian higher education institutions. The data were analyzed using exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Findings The analysis validates a seven-dimension model for assessing the entrepreneurial-engaged university. The results indicate that faculty members perceive the entrepreneurial and engagement dimensions of the third mission as a unified construct. Notably, the outreach dimension was consolidated: three constructs initially hypothesized as distinct could not be maintained as separate dimensions because inter-construct correlations of 0.887 and 0.900 exceeded the square roots of their respective average variances extracted. This finding suggests that faculty members do not cognitively distinguish among these aspects of the university's societal engagement. A second-order construct analysis further demonstrates that the seven validated dimensions are viewed by faculty as manifestations of a single, integrated higher-order construct, with all path coefficients positive and statistically significant. This perceptual integration aligns with theoretical arguments regarding the convergence of entrepreneurial and engaged university models and this study contributes a faculty-level analytical perspective to this discourse. Practical implications The validated scale provides university administrators with a diagnostic tool to assess their institution's internal capabilities, identify cultural and procedural bottlenecks and strategically guide investments to foster a more productive entrepreneurial environment. The second-order composite score additionally allows a single summary indicator of the institution's overall entrepreneurial-engaged orientation, complementing the seven-dimension profile. Originality/value This study provides empirical evidence that faculty perceive entrepreneurial and engaged orientations as a single integrated profile, and it delivers the first validated, perception-based scale designed to measure that profile.

title: THE CROSS-BORDER MIGRATION OF CHINA'S DIGITAL GOVERNANCE EXPERIENCE UNDER THE CHINA-ASEAN DIGITAL ECONOMY COOPERATION FRAMEWORK
journal: World Journal of Economics and Business Research
abstract: With the rapid development of digital technology, digital governance has become an important path to modernizing national governance and a key issue in global economic cooperation. Within the framework of China-ASEAN digital economy cooperation, regional cooperation practices centered on the "Digital Silk Road" have provided fertile ground for the cross-border transfer of China's digital governance experience. This paper, from the dialectical perspective of "development empowerment and sovereignty balance," systematically examines the core elements, current status, and pathways of the cross-border transfer of China's digital governance experience. The study finds that China's digital governance model, characterized by state-capacity leadership, infrastructure exports as a precursor, the promotion of technical standards as a link, and multi-party collaborative governance as a mechanism, has generated significant spillover effects in ASEAN's digital transformation process. This cooperation not only provides ASEAN countries with a development path different from the West and innovates the South-South digital cooperation paradigm, but also injects new momentum into the equitable and diversified transformation of the global digital governance system, highlighting the global governance significance of the "Chinese solution."

title: Smallholder farmers' preferences for public expenditure priorities to support maize productivity: evidence from a best–worst scaling experiment in western Kenya
abstract: Understanding how smallholder farmers want public resources allocated is essential for designing effective agricultural policies, especially in the maize sub-sector, where public interventions often compete for limited fiscal resources. This paper determined smallholder farmers’ preferences for enhancing maize productivity in western Kenya. Using survey data from 1,531 smallholder farmers, the study applied a best–worst scaling experiment in which farmers evaluated seven policy options across seven choice sets. Count analysis was used to rank aggregate policy preferences, while latent class modeling was used to identify heterogeneity in farmers’ preferences across classes. Results show that farmers strongly prefer improving access to soil-testing services, followed by increasing the quantity of subsidized fertilizer available to smallholder farmers, providing low-interest, unsecured loans, and increasing the number of well-trained and well-resourced public extension agents. Lower-ranked options included creating more market opportunities, improving access to agricultural lime, and improving rural roads and bridges. The latent class analysis further revealed heterogeneity in the preferences of smallholder farmers in western Kenya. The findings highlight the need to align public expenditure decisions with farmers’ expressed priorities, particularly when agricultural budgets are limited, and to design policy interventions that respond to the constraints farmers consider most urgent.

title: Processing capacity under complexity: an organizational information processing perspective on humanitarian supply chain performance
journal: Journal of Humanitarian Logistics and Supply Chain Management
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the role of processing capacity in shaping humanitarian supply chain performance under crisis conditions. Specifically, it examines how information processing capacity influences response performance and equity performance, and how environmental complexity and structural integration moderate these relationships. It also examines whether environmental complexity moderates the information processing capacity-equity performance relationship more strongly than the information processing capacity-response performance relationship. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT) and a contingency perspective, the research model is proposed and empirically evaluated using survey data collected from 600 professionals with relevant experience working in the humanitarian supply chain across India. The hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS. Findings The PLS-SEM results show that processing capacity has a significant positive effect on both response performance and equity performance. The environmental complexity amplifies the impact of processing capacity on both outcomes, but results confirm that it has stronger moderating effect for equity performance compared to response performance. Similarly, structural integration also significantly strengthens the relationship positively between processing capacity and both performance dimensions. Research limitations/implications First, this study extends OIPT to humanitarian supply chains by demonstrating that the relationship between information processing capacity and performance depends on environmental complexity. Second, it advances contingency-based reasoning by showing that environmental complexity strengthens the relationship between processing capacity and equity performance more than its relationship with response performance, suggesting that the value of processing capacity varies across humanitarian performance dimensions. Third, it extends OIPT by identifying structural integration, defined as the alignment between emergency and routine supply chain structures, as an organizational condition that strengthens the relationship between processing capacity and both response and equity performance. Practical implications The results and analysis presented in the study suggest that humanitarian organizations need to prioritize coordination among multiple actors, real-time information sharing, decentralized decision-making, and structural integration explained through the mechanisms of emergency and routine supply chain tasks. Originality/value This study contributes to the humanitarian supply chain literature by theorizing and empirically showing that processing capacity matters differently across humanitarian performance dimensions. It demonstrates that environmental complexity strengthens the processing capacity-performance relationship more strongly for equity performance than for response performance. The study also shows that structural integration enables humanitarian organizations to translate processing capacity into improved response and equity outcomes.
